# MASTER PROMPT: BUILD AN ULTRA-REALISTIC MOTORCYCLE RIDING EXPERIENCE IN DA NANG 3D

## 1. PROJECT CONTEXT

You are working on an existing 3D web experience:

https://danangbridges.netlify.app/

Project name: **Da Nang 3D – Explore the Bridges of Da Nang, Vietnam.**

The website allows visitors to explore Da Nang through an interactive 3D environment featuring famous landmarks and bridges, including:

- Dragon Bridge (Cầu Rồng).
- Han River Bridge (Cầu Sông Hàn).
- Tran Thi Ly Bridge (Cầu Trần Thị Lý).
- Thuan Phuoc Bridge (Cầu Thuận Phước).
- Other surrounding roads, buildings, river landscapes and city environments.

Existing experiences include:

- Paragliding.
- Car driving.
- Walking exploration.
- Guided tours and cinematic camera experiences.

The current interface already has a **Motorcycle / Xe máy** option marked as coming soon.

Your mission is to turn this placeholder into a fully functional, visually spectacular and immersive motorcycle riding experience.

### Most important objective

Do NOT create an independent motorcycle simulator or rebuild the existing website.

Integrate motorcycle riding as a native transportation mode within the existing 3D world.

The experience should make visitors feel as though they are genuinely riding a motorcycle through the streets and across the iconic bridges of Da Nang.

The result must be significantly more immersive than simply attaching a motorcycle model to a moving camera.

---

## 2. MANDATORY SUPERPOWERS WORKFLOW

This is an existing project with established architecture and multiple interactive experiences.

You MUST use the installed Superpowers workflow.

### Phase 0 – Project reconnaissance

Before proposing an implementation:

1. Read the existing project documentation and development instructions.
2. Inspect the complete repository structure.
3. Understand the rendering engine, scene management, camera systems, animation loops and existing player controls.
4. Study the current paragliding, car and walking implementations.
5. Identify how the existing application handles:
   - Vehicle movement.
   - Road and bridge geometry.
   - Camera positioning and transitions.
   - Collision detection.
   - Player identity and character models.
   - Multiplayer or shared-world synchronization, if available.
   - Weather and day/night transitions.
   - Sound effects and ambient audio.
   - Input handling on desktop and mobile.
   - UI and localization.
6. Identify available vehicle models, environmental assets, materials, shaders and reusable effects.
7. Run the existing application and establish a baseline for performance and functionality.

Do not assume that the deployed website reveals the full underlying architecture.

Base every technical decision on the actual source code.

**Important:** Do not prescribe a new architecture, state-management solution, data structure, physics engine or project folder structure before understanding the current implementation.

Prefer extending existing systems over introducing parallel implementations.

### Phase 1 – Brainstorming and Design Specification

Invoke the appropriate installed Superpowers brainstorming skill.

Analyze the project and develop a design for the motorcycle experience.

Present alternative approaches when there are meaningful architectural or gameplay trade-offs.

Provide a recommended approach with clear reasoning.

The design must cover:

- Overall motorcycle riding experience.
- Vehicle and rider presentation.
- Driving physics and movement.
- Camera system.
- Desktop and mobile controls.
- Environmental integration.
- Traffic and interactions.
- Audio design.
- Multiplayer integration, if supported by the existing project.
- Performance and compatibility.
- Testing and acceptance criteria.

Save the approved design document under the appropriate Superpowers specification directory.

Do not write implementation code at this stage.

Do not ask questions whose answers can be determined by inspecting the repository. Make reasonable technical decisions and clearly record assumptions. Ask only essential questions that materially change the experience.

Wait for design approval before proceeding.

### Phase 2 – Implementation Planning

After the design is approved, invoke the installed Superpowers writing-plans skill.

Produce a detailed, actionable implementation plan.

Requirements:

- Every task must reference actual files discovered during repository inspection.
- Break the implementation into small, independently testable tasks.
- Identify dependencies and implementation order.
- Include testing and verification instructions.
- Include performance validation.
- Include integration and regression checks.
- Avoid vague tasks such as "improve physics" or "make the graphics realistic".
- Define precisely what constitutes completion.

Save the plan under the appropriate Superpowers plans directory.

Review the plan against the approved specification.

Stop and request approval of the implementation plan before modifying application code.

### Phase 3 – Implementation

Once the plan is approved, execute it using the appropriate installed Superpowers implementation skills.

Follow test-driven development where appropriate.

Implement incrementally, verify every milestone and review the results before moving forward.

Do not skip tasks, silently change the approved design or implement unrelated features.

---

## 3. EXPERIENCE DESIGN – MOTORCYCLE RIDING

The motorcycle mode should feel like a real-world riding experience, not an arcade racing game.

The primary experience is free exploration of Da Nang.

Visitors should be able to ride through existing roads, explore the surroundings and cross the city's iconic bridges.

### 3.1 Motorcycle model

Create or integrate a highly realistic motorcycle model.

The preferred initial vehicle is a modern Vietnamese-style automatic scooter.

The motorcycle should have:

- Realistic body proportions.
- Detailed front and rear wheels.
- Realistic tires and tire textures.
- Functional-looking headlights and taillights.
- Turn signals.
- Mirrors.
- Handlebars.
- Brake components.
- Suspension.
- Seat and body panels.
- Realistic surface materials and reflections.

Avoid generic low-poly vehicle models.

Avoid recognizable manufacturer logos unless the project already has properly usable assets.

The motorcycle should look convincing from both first-person and third-person camera angles.

The model must be optimized for real-time WebGL rendering.

### 3.2 Rider and character animation

The motorcycle must have a convincing rider.

The rider should:

- Sit naturally on the motorcycle.
- Keep hands connected to the handlebars.
- Position feet appropriately.
- Lean naturally when turning.
- React to acceleration and braking.
- Maintain believable body posture while moving.

Avoid floating hands, disconnected limbs, clipping through the motorcycle or unnatural poses.

If the project already supports character selection or player identity, reuse the existing system.

Do not create a conflicting character management system.

If the experience supports multiplayer, other visitors must see a coherent motorcycle and rider rather than an invisible vehicle or an unrelated character.

### 3.3 First-person camera – The primary experience

The most important camera should create the feeling of sitting on the motorcycle.

The visitor should feel physically connected to the vehicle.

Include, where appropriate:

- Visible handlebars.
- Front motorcycle bodywork.
- Dashboard or instrument panel.
- Rear-view mirrors.
- Natural road perspective.
- Accurate sense of height above the road.
- Realistic perspective and field of view.

The camera must respond naturally to steering and acceleration.

When turning, the motorcycle and camera should exhibit believable lean behavior.

Add subtle physical feedback:

- Suspension response.
- Road vibration.
- Slight movement when accelerating.
- Natural camera inertia.
- Small environmental vibrations at high speeds.

Avoid excessive camera shake, unnatural movement or motion sickness.

### 3.4 Third-person camera

Provide an optional third-person follow camera.

The camera should follow the motorcycle smoothly while maintaining a cinematic viewing angle.

It should:

- Track the motorcycle without excessive lag.
- Avoid clipping through buildings and surrounding geometry.
- Maintain a sensible distance.
- React smoothly to turning.
- Show the rider and motorcycle clearly.

Allow switching between first-person and third-person views without interrupting the ride.

---

## 4. REALISTIC MOTORCYCLE PHYSICS

This is one of the most important parts of the experience.

The motorcycle must behave like an actual road vehicle.

Implement realistic and responsive:

- Acceleration.
- Deceleration.
- Steering.
- Braking.
- Turning radius.
- Leaning when cornering.
- Suspension movement.
- Wheel rotation.
- Tire-road interaction.
- Weight and inertia.
- Speed-dependent steering sensitivity.

Avoid instantaneous changes in speed or direction.

The motorcycle should feel heavier at higher speeds and more responsive at lower speeds.

When accelerating, the vehicle should exhibit subtle weight transfer.

When braking, the vehicle should decelerate progressively rather than stopping instantly.

When turning, the motorcycle should lean naturally instead of rotating like a rigid object.

The physics should be believable but still enjoyable for casual visitors.

This is a sightseeing experience, not a demanding professional motorcycle simulator.

### Road interaction

The motorcycle must remain physically connected to the road surface.

Pay particular attention to:

- Road elevation changes.
- Bridge ramps.
- Slopes.
- Uneven road geometry.
- Road boundaries.
- Curbs.
- Bridge barriers.
- Road intersections.
- Different road surfaces.

Prevent the motorcycle from accidentally driving across sidewalks, floating above roads or falling through bridge geometry.

Implement appropriate collision and recovery behavior.

If the motorcycle leaves a valid driving surface, provide a natural recovery mechanism rather than leaving the visitor stuck indefinitely.

---

## 5. DA NANG ENVIRONMENT INTEGRATION

This feature must showcase the existing Da Nang environment.

The motorcycle must travel within the same 3D world as the other transportation modes.

### Important landmarks

Ensure the experience integrates naturally with existing locations:

- Cầu Rồng.
- Cầu Sông Hàn.
- Cầu Trần Thị Lý.
- Cầu Thuận Phước.
- Surrounding roads and riverfront areas.
- Existing city buildings and landmarks.

Do not create disconnected duplicate bridge environments.

Reuse actual existing scene geometry and road infrastructure whenever possible.

Inspect whether the road network currently connects these areas sufficiently for continuous motorcycle riding.

If there are missing or incomplete road connections, identify them in the specification and propose the smallest viable improvements.

Do not rebuild the entire city.

### Road realism

The road surface must look convincing from the rider's perspective.

Improve or reuse:

- Asphalt textures.
- Road markings.
- Lane separation.
- Directional arrows.
- Crosswalks.
- Roadside curbs.
- Streetlights.
- Traffic signs.
- Sidewalks.
- Roadside barriers.
- Drainage and environmental details where appropriate.

Ensure the motorcycle follows the correct Vietnamese right-hand traffic orientation.

Avoid placing road markings or street furniture arbitrarily.

### Environmental realism

Preserve the existing city atmosphere.

The visitor should be able to appreciate:

- The Han River.
- Bridge architecture.
- Riverfront buildings.
- City skylines.
- Street lighting.
- Surrounding traffic.
- Reflections from the water.

The scenery should remain visually coherent when observed at motorcycle speed.

---

## 6. TRAFFIC AND LIVING CITY

A realistic motorcycle experience needs a living environment.

Reuse existing vehicle and traffic systems whenever possible.

Other vehicles should:

- Follow appropriate road directions.
- Move at believable speeds.
- Maintain reasonable spacing.
- Respect road geometry.
- Avoid unrealistic movement.
- Avoid appearing suddenly in front of the player.

Include realistic ambient city movement where supported by existing systems.

However, traffic must not constantly block the visitor or make the experience frustrating.

The objective is to create the feeling of riding through an active Vietnamese city.

The motorcycle should coexist naturally with the existing cars, traffic and other visitors.

Do not turn this feature into a full traffic simulation project.

Prioritize the motorcycle experience itself.

---

## 7. AUDIO DESIGN – EXTREMELY IMPORTANT

Audio must be designed as an integral part of the experience.

The motorcycle should not sound like a single looping engine recording.

Build a layered and responsive audio experience.

### Motorcycle audio

Include:

- Engine idling.
- Engine acceleration.
- Engine sound changing with RPM and speed.
- Engine deceleration.
- Tire contact with asphalt.
- Subtle suspension and road vibration sounds.
- Brake sounds where appropriate.
- Horn.
- Turn signal indicators.
- Starting and stopping sounds.

The engine audio must dynamically respond to acceleration and deceleration.

Avoid abrupt audio transitions, repetitive loops that are easy to recognize, distorted audio and sudden volume spikes.

### Environmental audio

Include spatial environmental sounds such as:

- Wind that becomes stronger as the motorcycle accelerates.
- Traffic passing nearby.
- Other motorcycles.
- Cars and horns.
- City ambience.
- River ambience.
- Bridge-specific environmental atmosphere.

Audio positioning should change naturally based on the motorcycle's location.

When entering an enclosed environment such as an existing tunnel, reuse or implement appropriate acoustic transitions if feasible.

Make audio transitions smooth and avoid overlapping or leaking sounds after switching modes.

Provide independent sound controls following the existing website's audio conventions.

---

## 8. WEATHER AND TIME-OF-DAY INTEGRATION

One of the project's existing strengths is its interactive weather and lighting system.

The motorcycle mode must integrate with it.

Do not build an entirely separate weather system.

### Daytime

- Natural sunlight.
- Realistic road shading.
- Proper reflections on motorcycle surfaces.
- Realistic environmental lighting.

### Nighttime

- Functional motorcycle headlights.
- Rear lights.
- Instrument panel illumination.
- Streetlight reflections.
- Realistic nighttime city atmosphere.
- Appropriate exposure and visibility.

### Rain

Rain should dramatically change the riding experience.

Include where supported:

- Wet asphalt.
- Reflections of streetlights and buildings.
- Reflections from motorcycle headlights.
- Tire spray.
- Rain particles.
- Ambient rain sound.
- Appropriate camera and environmental effects.
- Subtle changes to road traction.

Avoid unrealistic mirror-like reflections across every surface.

The motorcycle must remain controllable in adverse weather.

The existing storm and weather scenarios should remain compatible with this new mode where practical.

---

## 9. CONTROL SYSTEM

Inspect the existing car and walking control implementations before defining the final motorcycle controls.

Reuse established input conventions wherever practical.

Suggested desktop controls:

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| W / Up Arrow | Accelerate |
| S / Down Arrow | Brake |
| A / Left Arrow | Steer left |
| D / Right Arrow | Steer right |
| H | Horn |
| Mouse drag | Look around |
| Esc | Exit motorcycle mode |

The final control mapping should account for the existing vehicle control system and avoid conflicts with camera controls.

### Mobile support

Design an appropriate touch interface if the project's existing mobile capabilities allow it.

Include:

- Acceleration control.
- Brake control.
- Steering controls.
- Camera view switching.
- Exit button.
- Optional horn control.

Touch controls must be comfortable, responsive and visually integrated with the experience.

Do not let the controls obscure too much of the 3D environment.

Handle different screen sizes and mobile safe areas.

---

## 10. MOTORCYCLE UI / HUD

Create a clean, immersive and unobtrusive interface.

The HUD should support riding rather than distract from the environment.

Consider:

- Speedometer.
- Gear or automatic transmission indication if appropriate.
- Engine status.
- Headlight status.
- Camera switching.
- Horn.
- Brake and accelerator controls.
- Exit experience.

Use a visual style consistent with the existing Da Nang 3D website.

The speedometer should respond to actual vehicle speed, not a decorative animation.

The HUD should be available in the existing website languages using the established localization system.

Do not introduce a completely different design language.

---

## 11. MULTIPLAYER AND SHARED-WORLD COMPATIBILITY

Inspect the current shared-world architecture before designing this functionality.

If the project supports multiple visitors in a shared environment:

- Other visitors should see the motorcycle and its rider.
- Motorcycle position and orientation should synchronize correctly.
- Movement should appear smooth for remote visitors.
- Rider identity should remain consistent with the existing system.
- Vehicle transitions should not leave stale avatars or duplicate vehicles.
- Exiting motorcycle mode should cleanly update the shared world.

Reuse the current networking and synchronization mechanisms.

Do not introduce an independent multiplayer implementation.

If multiplayer synchronization is not currently supported for vehicle modes, identify the actual limitation and propose an implementation that fits the existing architecture.

The single-player experience must still work when the shared-world server is unavailable, following the project's existing offline fallback behavior.

---

## 12. PERFORMANCE AND TECHNICAL QUALITY

This is a browser-based real-time 3D application.

Visual quality must not come at the cost of unusable performance.

Pay particular attention to:

- Draw calls.
- Polygon count.
- Texture memory.
- Shadow rendering.
- Dynamic lighting.
- Reflection calculations.
- Particle systems.
- Audio processing.
- Animation updates.
- Physics calculations.
- Network update frequency.

Reuse existing rendering infrastructure.

Use appropriate level of detail, frustum culling, instancing, resource reuse and optimized asset loading when supported by the existing architecture.

Avoid unnecessary dependencies.

Do not add expensive post-processing effects merely to make screenshots look impressive.

Make sure that:

- GPU resources are disposed correctly.
- Event listeners are cleaned up.
- Animation loops do not duplicate.
- Audio is stopped or released when leaving the mode.
- Switching between transportation modes does not cause memory leaks.
- The motorcycle does not negatively affect the existing car, paragliding or walking modes.

Establish and compare performance against the existing project baseline.

Target smooth performance on capable desktop devices and stable performance on reasonably capable mobile devices.

Provide graceful degradation when hardware cannot support the highest visual settings.

---

## 13. TESTING AND ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

The feature is not complete just because a motorcycle model appears on the screen.

The following must be verified.

### Functional tests

1. The Xe máy option is no longer marked as coming soon.
2. Selecting it correctly enters motorcycle mode.
3. The motorcycle spawns at a valid road location.
4. Acceleration and braking work correctly.
5. Steering works at both low and high speeds.
6. Leaning and suspension behave naturally.
7. First-person camera works correctly.
8. Third-person camera works correctly.
9. Camera switching is smooth.
10. The motorcycle can travel on the available bridge and road network.
11. The player cannot easily drive through barriers or fall through the environment.
12. Horn and other audio controls work.
13. Day/night and weather systems integrate correctly.
14. Desktop controls work.
15. Mobile controls work where supported.
16. Multiplayer works if supported.
17. Exiting motorcycle mode restores the previous application state correctly.
18. Re-entering motorcycle mode does not duplicate listeners, audio or rendering loops.

### Visual quality tests

Inspect the experience at:

- Low speed.
- High speed.
- During turns.
- While braking.
- Crossing bridge ramps.
- Daytime.
- Nighttime.
- Rain.
- First-person camera.
- Third-person camera.

Look for:

- Model clipping.
- Unnatural rider posture.
- Floating wheels.
- Incorrect road alignment.
- Camera jitter.
- Unnatural shadows.
- Poor reflections.
- Low-quality road appearance.
- Visual inconsistencies with existing city assets.

### Regression tests

Verify that existing experiences remain fully functional:

- Paragliding.
- Car driving.
- Walking.
- Guided tours.
- Existing bridge camera experiences.
- Existing weather and lighting controls.

Do not sacrifice existing functionality to implement the motorcycle mode.

---

## 14. SCOPE MANAGEMENT

Focus on delivering one excellent motorcycle experience.

Do not expand the project into:

- A motorcycle racing game.
- A vehicle dealership.
- A multi-vehicle purchasing system.
- A complex motorcycle tuning simulator.
- A complete traffic simulation engine.
- An entirely new open-world map.
- Unrelated website redesigns.

One excellent, realistic motorcycle is preferable to several poorly implemented vehicles.

Additional motorcycles and gameplay features can be considered in future iterations.

---

## 15. SESSION CONTINUITY AND RECOVERY

This project may require multiple Claude sessions.

The implementation must remain understandable after closing Claude, restarting the computer or starting a new session.

Use the project's documentation and Superpowers workflow to preserve:

- Approved specifications.
- Approved implementation plan.
- Important architectural discoveries.
- Technical decisions and their reasoning.
- Completed tasks.
- Outstanding tasks.
- Known issues.
- Test results.
- Exact next implementation step.

Maintain an appropriate progress document in the repository.

When resuming work:

1. Read the project instructions.
2. Read the approved specification.
3. Read the implementation plan.
4. Read the progress document.
5. Inspect the current Git status and actual code.
6. Verify which tasks have already been completed.
7. Continue from the next incomplete task.

Never assume that a previous session completed something merely because it appears in the plan.

Do not repeat completed work or overwrite valid changes.

---

## 16. FINAL QUALITY BAR

Think like a combination of:

- Senior Three.js / WebGL Engineer.
- Vehicle Physics Engineer.
- Real-Time 3D Environment Artist.
- Technical Game Designer.
- Sound Designer.
- Performance Optimization Engineer.
- Software Architect.

The final result should feel like a premium interactive 3D motorcycle sightseeing experience.

Imagine a visitor starting the motorcycle, hearing the engine come alive, gently accelerating along the road, feeling the motorcycle lean through a turn, approaching Dragon Bridge, hearing the surrounding traffic and wind, and seeing the illuminated city reflected on the Han River at night.

Every visual, physical and audio interaction should reinforce the feeling of actually being there.

**Immersion, realism, responsiveness and environmental integration take priority over adding unnecessary features.**

Do not settle for a basic implementation just because the motorcycle can move.

---

## YOUR FIRST ACTION

Start by invoking the appropriate Superpowers workflow.

Inspect the actual repository and existing vehicle modes.

Then present your findings, recommended design approach, trade-offs and proposed scope.

Create the design specification first. Obtain approval, then create the implementation plan.

**Do not modify application source code until the design and implementation plan have been reviewed and approved.**

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

**Tôi hiểu yêu cầu thế này:** biến thẻ "Xe máy — Sắp có" thành chế độ lái xe tay ga thật sự nhập vai trong chính thế giới hiện có. Góc nhìn thứ nhất là chính (thấy ghi đông, đồng hồ, gương), có thêm góc thứ ba. Xe phải nghiêng khi vào cua, có người lái ngồi đúng tư thế, âm thanh nhiều lớp, ăn khớp ngày/đêm/mưa và nhiều người. Mục tiêu là cảm giác "đang ở đó", không phải game đua.

**Những gì tôi thấy trong repo có ảnh hưởng tới việc này:**
- **Tái dùng được gần hết chế độ Ô tô (D-034):** mạng đường khoảng 150 ô qua 4 cầu và hầm, va chạm, sơ tán nhịp quay Cầu sông Hàn, HUD, cảm ứng, sảnh 5 chỗ. Xe máy nên là một phương tiện thứ hai trên nền đó, không phải hệ song song.
- **Người lái đã có tiền lệ:** người treo dù (D-035) dùng đoạn `sit`, IK tay nắm quai và lò xo phản ứng theo rẽ / tăng giảm tốc. Đó đúng là thứ người ngồi xe máy cần.
- **Phần phải làm mới:** camera góc nhìn thứ nhất, nghiêng xe, nhún giảm xóc, mặt đường ướt và bụi nước bánh xe. Âm thanh hiện chỉ có 2 dao động tổng hợp, chưa có lớp nào.
- **Nhiều người:** cần thêm loại chỗ mới ở Worker `danang-sky`, tức phải deploy và tôi sẽ hỏi riêng lúc đó.
- **Nhánh:** nhánh hiện tại `feature/ven-song-chan-thuc` đang dở, có `src/config.ts` chưa commit, và chưa có phần chọn nhân vật (D-039) của `main`. Tôi sẽ làm xe máy trên nhánh mới từ `main`, trong worktree riêng, không đụng việc ven sông.

Chỗ nào tôi hiểu sai thì anh sửa giúp.

**Một câu hỏi quyết định nhiều nhất: mô hình xe lấy từ đâu?**
1. **Mô hình ngoài có giấy phép CC BY / CC0 (tôi đề xuất):** xử lý qua Blender như VF 3, gỡ logo và biển số, tách bánh / phuộc / ghi đông. Chỉ cách này đạt mức "rất thật" khi nhìn sát ở góc thứ nhất; đổi lại phải ghi công và tải thêm khoảng 1 MB.
2. **Dựng bằng script Blender** (như `gen:buildings`): không vướng giấy phép, nhưng thân vỏ cong của xe tay ga sẽ trông cứng.
3. **Dựng bằng code:** nhẹ nhất, nhưng không đạt yêu cầu "không low-poly".

Anh chọn cách 1 chứ? Nếu có, anh đã có sẵn mô hình ưng ý, hay để tôi tìm vài ứng viên kèm giấy phép cho anh chọn?

Tôi đã tìm trên Sketchfab. Tôi chỉ đọc được trang mô tả, chưa xem được lưới thật vì tải về cần đăng nhập.

## Mô hình xe

| Ứng viên | Giấy phép | Tam giác | Nhận xét |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Honda SH 125](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/honda-sh-125-07e1bc00d26f44958c0fa8062ce94e36) (steveconrad82) | CC BY | 92,3 nghìn | **Tôi chọn.** Dáng xe tay ga hiện đại, quen ở Việt Nam. |
| [Honda PCX 2023](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/REDACTED) (parchin666) | CC BY | 149,9 nghìn | Dự phòng. Tên tệp gợi ý lưới quét / tự sinh, có thể khó tách bánh và ghi đông. |
| [Honda Spacy](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/honda-spacy-2225281a19c74c76a711c673c3b9b35e) (RusikMDLR) | CC BY | 90,7 nghìn | Loại: xe đời 1980. |

Các kết quả khác đều không dùng được: quá thô (1–2 nghìn tam giác), kiểu viễn tưởng, hoặc cấm dùng thương mại. Tôi không tìm thấy xe VinFast nào có giấy phép mở.

Hai điều cần anh biết trước:
- **Logo:** tôi sẽ gỡ logo và biển số, trong giao diện chỉ gọi là "xe tay ga". Dáng xe vẫn nhận ra là SH, giống như VF 3 hiện nay.
- **Chưa kiểm được lưới:** bánh, phuộc, ghi đông có tách rời được không thì phải mở tệp mới biết. Nếu SH không tách được, tôi chuyển sang PCX.

**Việc cần anh làm:** tải SH 125 (và PCX nếu tiện) ở định dạng glTF/GLB, đặt vào `scripts/bike/`. Tôi không dùng tài khoản của anh để tải.

## Cách dựng

1. **Thư mục `src/explore/bike/` riêng, dùng lại nền của Ô tô (tôi đề xuất).** Mạng đường, vật cản, va chạm, sơ tán nhịp quay và cần gạt cảm ứng giữ nguyên, chỉ thêm tham số kích thước thân xe. Phần viết mới là chuyển động có nghiêng và giảm xóc, camera góc nhìn thứ nhất và thứ ba, người lái, âm thanh, HUD. Chế độ Ô tô gần như không bị đụng.
2. **Gộp Ô tô và xe máy thành một khung "phương tiện" chung.** Gọn về lâu dài, nhưng phải sửa sâu chế độ Ô tô trong khi bộ test nặng của nó chưa chạy trọn lần nào, nên rủi ro hỏng cái đang chạy.
3. **Chép nguyên thư mục `drive/` rồi sửa.** Nhanh nhất, nhưng hai bản va chạm và mạng đường sẽ lệch nhau dần.

Các lựa chọn kèm theo, anh sửa nếu không đồng ý:
- **Người lái:** nhân vật Rocketbox theo lựa chọn nam / nữ ở sảnh (D-039), đội mũ bảo hiểm, ngồi bằng tư thế `sit` và tay bám ghi đông bằng IK như người treo dù.
- **Nhiều người:** dùng chung 5 chỗ "lái" với Ô tô, thêm một trường loại xe. Worker đổi ít, khách cũ vẫn chạy, người đi xe máy và ô tô thấy nhau.
- **Âm thanh:** tiếng máy dùng đoạn thu thật giấy phép CC0 (nổ cầm chừng / thấp / cao, trộn theo vòng tua mô phỏng hộp số vô cấp). Gió, lốp, xi nhan, còi thì tổng hợp như hiện nay. Tổng hợp thuần không ra được tiếng máy xăng thật.
- **Mưa:** mặt đường ướt làm bằng shader (bóng hơn, vệt đèn kéo dài như vệt trên sông), bụi nước bánh xe là một lưới hạt. Không dùng phản chiếu thật và không thêm đèn, để giữ số lệnh vẽ.

Anh đồng ý cách 1 và bốn lựa chọn trên chứ? Sau đó tôi viết bản thiết kế đầy đủ; một reviewer sẽ đọc trước và tôi có thể quay lại hỏi thêm một lần.

# Chế độ lái xe máy (xe tay ga) — thiết kế

_Ngày: 2026-11-14 · Quyết định: D-040 · Nhánh: `feature/xe-may` (từ `main` `a66989b`) · Trạng thái: chờ người dùng duyệt_

Ghi chú về nguồn gốc từng điều: **(ND)** = người dùng nói / đã duyệt trong buổi brainstorming; **(Claude)** = lựa chọn của Claude, người dùng chưa phản đối nhưng cũng chưa duyệt riêng; không ghi gì = suy ra trực tiếp từ mã hiện có.

## 1. Ý định

Thẻ "Xe máy — Sắp có" ở màn chọn (`index.html` `data-pick="bike"`, khóa `exBike` / `exSoon`) trở thành một chế độ khám phá thật: người xem ngồi lên một chiếc xe tay ga, nghe máy nổ, vặn ga chạy trên chính mạng đường của chế độ Ô tô, nghiêng xe qua khúc rẽ, qua bốn cây cầu và Hầm vượt sông Hàn (phương án đề xuất), ngày, đêm và mưa. **(ND)**

Vì sao: đây là cách người Đà Nẵng thật sự đi trong thành phố; người dùng muốn cảm giác "đang ở đó", vượt hẳn mức "gắn mô hình xe vào camera chạy". Ưu tiên theo thứ tự: nhập vai, chân thực, phản hồi nhanh, ăn khớp với cảnh hiện có. **(ND)**

## 2. Mục tiêu / không làm / thất bại

**Mục tiêu**
1. Thẻ Xe máy mở được; vào bằng thẻ hoặc `?explore=bike`.
2. Góc nhìn thứ nhất là trải nghiệm chính: thấy ghi đông, mặt đồng hồ, gương, hai tay; có góc nhìn thứ ba; đổi qua lại không ngắt chuyến đi. **(ND)**
3. Xe nghiêng khi rẽ, có quán tính, nặng tay ở tốc độ cao, nhạy ở tốc độ thấp; nhún giảm xóc; bánh lăn và bám mặt đường trên dốc cầu. **(ND)**
4. Người lái có xương ngồi đúng tư thế, tay bám ghi đông, chân đặt sàn xe, nghiêng theo xe, phản ứng khi tăng tốc / phanh. **(ND)**
5. Âm thanh nhiều lớp phản hồi theo ga và tốc độ. **(ND)**
6. Ăn khớp ngày / đêm / thời tiết sẵn có; mưa đổi cảm giác lái. **(ND)**
7. Nhiều người: người khác thấy xe + người lái; ngoại tuyến vẫn lái một mình.
8. Máy tính và điện thoại; 9 ngôn ngữ.

**Không làm**
- Không đua, không chọn nhiều xe, không độ xe, không bản đồ mới. **(ND)**
- Không dựng mô phỏng giao thông mới; dùng xe tự động sẵn có. **(ND)**
- Không gương chiếu hậu phản chiếu thật (mỗi gương là một lượt vẽ cảnh) — gương dùng vật liệu phản chiếu trời giả. **(Claude)**
- Không thêm biển báo, vạch qua đường, mũi tên mới trên toàn mạng đường; chỉ tăng chi tiết nhựa đường nhìn gần và mặt đường ướt (§9). **(Claude)**
- Không giọt nước trên kính / màn hình ở góc nhìn thứ nhất. **(Claude)**
- Không ngã xe, không hư hỏng: đâm vật cản thì dừng / trượt dọc như ô tô.
- Không gộp chế độ Ô tô và xe máy thành một khung chung (cách 2 đã loại, §4).

**Thất bại dù chạy được**
- Tay rời ghi đông, bánh lơ lửng hoặc chìm, người lái xuyên thân xe.
- Camera rung gây chóng mặt; đường chân trời lắc theo từng phím.
- Xe quay như một khối cứng (không nghiêng), hoặc đổi tốc độ / hướng tức thời.
- Tiếng máy là một vòng lặp nghe ra ngay, giật khi đổi lớp, còn kêu sau khi thoát.
- Chế độ Ô tô, Dù lượn, Đi dạo, Tour đổi hành vi; góc nhìn cũ tăng lệnh vẽ; chuỗi `rand()` đổi.

## 3. Hiện trạng (đã đọc mã, `main` `a66989b`)

- **Chế độ Ô tô (D-034)** `src/explore/drive/`: `net.ts` + `roadData.ts` (≈ 150 ô mặt đường nhiều tầng, cổng nhịp quay), `solids.ts` + `sceneSolids.ts` (vật cản), `collide.ts` (thân xe chữ nhật 9 điểm mẫu, `drMove` / `drFits` / `drSegClear`), `motion.ts` (mô hình xe đạp động học, `drStep`, sơ tán `drEvacStep`), `camera.ts` (sau xe, kẹp trần hầm), `hud.ts` (đồng hồ DOM, bản đồ nhỏ), `touch.ts`, `keys.ts`, `sound.ts` (2 dao động + còi, cổng `sfxPort` / `extPort`), `car.ts` / `cars.ts` (glb + hình tạm, làm nóng shader), `index.ts` (điều phối, `cam.mode = 'car'`). Kích thước thân xe là hằng số cấp module đọc `CONFIG.drive.car` trong `collide.ts` và `motion.ts`.
- **Người có xương**: Đi dạo `src/explore/stroll/{rig,anim,avatars,char}.ts` với `public/people/p0.glb` (nam) / `p3.glb` (nữ) sau D-039; người treo dù `src/explore/pilot/{rig,ik,react,bones,gear}.ts` (đoạn `sit`, IK hai khớp tay, lò xo phản ứng theo rẽ / tăng giảm tốc / gió, trang bị dựng bằng code thành SkinnedMesh).
- **Nhiều người** `src/explore/multi/`, Worker `server/multi/` (`danang-sky`): ba loại chỗ `fly` / `walk` / `drive`, mỗi loại 5; `join` kind `drive`; `pos` người lái `[slot, x, y, z, yaw, v, st, ts]`; `lobby.drivers`; `ch` (nhân vật) đi theo `join` kind `walk` và `lobby.walkers`.
- **Xe tự động**: `common/trafficQuery.ts` `trNearby()` trả hộp các xe gần; đã có xe tay ga hình khối (`common/vehicles/shapes.ts`).
- **Âm thanh** `src/audio/index.ts`: toàn bộ tổng hợp bằng Web Audio, không có tệp âm thanh hiệu ứng nào; `public/voice/` có mp3 thuyết minh.
- **Chưa có ở đâu**: camera góc nhìn thứ nhất, nghiêng xe, giảm xóc, mặt đường ướt, bụi nước, tiếng theo vị trí.

## 4. Các cách đã cân nhắc

1. **`src/explore/bike/` riêng, dùng lại nền của Ô tô** — _đã chọn_ **(ND)**. Mạng đường, vật cản, va chạm, sơ tán, cần gạt cảm ứng, bản đồ nhỏ dùng nguyên; chỉ thêm tham số "thân xe" cho `collide.ts` / `drEvacStep`. Viết mới: chuyển động có nghiêng, giảm xóc, hai camera, mô hình + người lái, âm thanh, phần HUD riêng. Ô tô gần như không bị đụng.
2. **Gộp Ô tô + xe máy thành khung "phương tiện" chung** — loại: sửa sâu chế độ Ô tô trong khi `test:drive` chưa từng chạy trọn; rủi ro hỏng cái đang chạy.
3. **Chép `drive/` rồi sửa** — loại: hai bản va chạm / mạng đường lệch nhau dần.

Kèm theo, đã duyệt **(ND)**: mô hình ngoài CC BY; người lái Rocketbox theo lựa chọn nam / nữ; dùng chung 5 chỗ lái với Ô tô; tiếng máy bằng đoạn thu CC0, phần còn lại tổng hợp; mưa bằng shader + một lưới hạt, không phản chiếu thật, không đèn mới.

## 5. Xe

### 5.1 Mô hình
- Nguồn **(ND chọn "bạn có thể chọn", Claude chọn)**: "Honda SH 125" của steveconrad82, Sketchfab, CC BY 4.0, 92,3 nghìn tam giác (`https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/honda-sh-125-07e1bc00d26f44958c0fa8062ce94e36`). Dự phòng: "Honda PCX 2023 Scooter" của parchin666, CC BY 4.0, 149,9 nghìn tam giác. **Chưa ai mở lưới**: giấy phép và số tam giác đọc từ trang, phải kiểm lại trên trang lúc tải; cấu trúc lưới (bánh / phuộc / ghi đông có tách được không) chỉ biết khi mở tệp. Người dùng tải tệp nguồn về `scripts/bike/` (Sketchfab cần đăng nhập). SH không tách được ⇒ thử PCX; cả hai không được ⇒ dừng, hỏi người dùng.
- Xử lý: `npm run gen:bike` → `scripts/bike/convert.py` (Blender 4.5 qua `scripts/people/blender.mjs`, mẫu `scripts/car/convert.py`): xóa logo, chữ hãng, biển số; giảm tam giác; tách các nút `body`, `front` (phuộc + ghi đông + chắn bùn trước + gương + cụm đồng hồ, gốc đặt trên trục cổ lái), `wheelF`, `wheelR`; gộp vật liệu về: sơn (màu theo slot như ô tô), nhựa đen, kim loại sáng, kính đèn (emissive), mặt đồng hồ (nhận texture canvas), mặt gương.
- Trần: `public/bike/scooter.glb` ≤ 1,2 MB, ≤ 30 000 tam giác; có test kiểm. **(Claude; ô tô là 0,88 MB / 18 000)**
- Ghi công: `public/bike/LICENSE-Scooter.txt`, README, dòng `#bkCredit` ở màn chọn / sảnh (CC BY buộc ghi tên tác phẩm gốc nên chữ "Honda SH 125" chỉ xuất hiện ở dòng ghi công). Trong giao diện gọi là "Xe máy" / "xe tay ga".
- Hình tạm khi glb chậm / lỗi / quá `CONFIG.bike.model.timeoutMs`: dựng bằng code từ hình xe tay ga sẵn có ở `common/vehicles/shapes.ts`, cùng kích thước va chạm.
- Lệnh vẽ: xe của mình ≤ 6, người lái ≤ 2 (thân + mũ / phụ kiện gộp); xe người khác ≤ 4 kể cả người lái. Chưa có xe máy nào thì +0 ở mọi góc cũ (nhóm chỉ vào cảnh khi có xe, như `drCars`).

### 5.2 Thông số (`CONFIG.bike`, mọi dòng có chú thích tiếng Việt + đơn vị + nguồn hoặc `(ước lượng)`)
Số của Honda SH 125i theo trí nhớ của Claude, **phải đối chiếu nguồn công bố khi lập plan** rồi ghi nguồn: dài 2,090 m, rộng 0,739 m, cao 1,129 m, cơ sở 1,353 m, yên cao 0,799 m, bánh 16 inch (đường kính ngoài ≈ 0,57 m trước / ≈ 0,60 m sau), 134 kg. Ước lượng: `vMax` 25 m/s (90 km/h), 0–50 km/h ≈ 5 s, phanh 7 m/s² (khô), nhả ga 1,2 m/s² (hãm động cơ + ly tâm nhả), nghiêng tối đa 35° khô.

### 5.3 Chuyển động (`src/explore/bike/motion.ts`, không import three, test được bằng Node)
Giữ khung của `drStep`: bước con ≤ `sim.dt`, dời thân bằng `drMove`, mất phần tốc độ hướng vào vật cản, kết quả không phụ thuộc tần số khung, không cấp phát mỗi khung. Khác ô tô ở chỗ **người chơi điều khiển độ nghiêng, không phải góc lái**:
- Trạng thái thêm `lean` (rad, dương = nghiêng trái), `leanV`, `susF` / `susR` (hành trình giảm xóc trước / sau, m), `rpm`, `throttle` đã làm mượt, `sig` (xi nhan −1 / 0 / 1).
- Tốc độ ≥ `vBlend` (≈ 4 m/s): phím trái / phải đặt độ nghiêng đích `±leanMax(v)`; `lean` tiến về đích như hệ lò xo giảm chấn tới hạn với tần số giảm theo tốc độ (nặng tay khi nhanh); tốc độ đổi hướng = `g · tan(lean) / v`. `leanMax(v)` kẹp thêm sao cho bán kính rẽ không nhỏ hơn bán kính hình học.
- Tốc độ thấp: trộn dần sang lái bằng góc lái như mô hình xe đạp động học của ô tô (bán kính quay nhỏ ≈ 2 m), độ nghiêng nhỏ theo `atan(v² κ / g)`. Đứng yên xe thẳng đứng (chống chân không mô phỏng).
- Ga: đường cong tăng tốc kiểu `drAccel` với số của xe máy; ga làm mượt (`throttle`) để không đổi gia tốc tức thời. Phanh tăng dần trong ≈ 0,15 s. Space = phanh gấp (cả hai phanh), không trượt.
- Lùi: xe tay ga không có số lùi. Giữ S khi đã đứng: dắt lùi ≤ 1 m/s (cần để thoát góc kẹt). **(Claude)**
- Vòng tua (cho âm thanh và kim đồng hồ): mô hình hộp số vô cấp — cầm chừng khi đứng; dưới ≈ 12 km/h ly tâm trượt (tua lên theo ga, xe mới nhích); vặn ga thì tua nhảy lên vùng công suất rồi giữ gần đó trong khi tốc độ tăng; nhả ga tua rơi về mức tỉ lệ tốc độ.
- Giảm xóc (chỉ hình + camera, không đổi quỹ đạo): mỗi đầu xe một lò xo giảm chấn; đầu vào là gia tốc dọc (phanh ⇒ chúi đầu, ga ⇒ nhún đuôi), đổi độ dốc tại mối nối ô mặt đường (lên / xuống dốc cầu), và nhiễu mặt đường biên độ nhỏ theo tốc độ từ `rng(seed)` riêng.
- Mưa (`weatherU` / preset thời tiết hiện có): nghiêng tối đa 35° → 27°, phanh 7 → 5,5 m/s² (ước lượng), chuyển mượt theo cường độ mưa. Gió bão đẩy nhẹ độ nghiêng (≤ 2°), không làm mất lái.
- Thân va chạm: chữ nhật dài × rộng của xe máy (không nới theo độ nghiêng **(Claude)**), chiều cao tính cả người lái (≈ 1,7 m) cho vật cản theo cao độ. `collide.ts` và `drEvacStep` nhận kích thước thân qua tham số, mặc định là VF 3; **`test:drive:unit` phải giữ 124/124 không sửa kỳ vọng**.
- Hồi phục: phím R (và nút trên HUD) đặt xe về tim làn gần nhất của ô mặt đường gần nhất, hướng theo chiều làn bên phải, đứng yên. Gợi ý "bấm R" hiện khi xe bị chặn mà vẫn vặn ga quá 3 s. Rơi khỏi mọi ô (dữ liệu sai) ⇒ tự về chỗ xuất phát như ô tô.
- Xuất phát: chỗ của slot như ô tô (`drSpawnPose`), trên Cầu Rồng chiều đi Đông, đi bên phải.
- Xe tự động: như ô tô (mình lao vào thì bị chặn, nó chạy tới thì đi xuyên). Sơ tán nhịp quay Cầu sông Hàn: dùng `drEvacStep` với thân xe máy.

## 6. Người lái (`src/explore/bike/rider.ts` + dùng lại `pilot/ik.ts`, `stroll/rig.ts`)

- Tư thế ngồi: **để người làm quyết** giữa (a) thêm đoạn một khung `ride` vào `p0` / `p3` qua `gen:people` từ nguồn ngồi của Rocketbox (như `sit` của `pilot.glb`), và (b) đặt tư thế nền bằng bảng góc khớp trong code. Tiêu chí chọn: (a) nếu chạy lại `gen:people` cho kết quả tất định và không đổi các đoạn sẵn có (`test:stroll:unit` giữ nguyên); không thì (b).
- IK hai khớp: hai tay tới hai tay nắm (điểm neo là nút con của `front`, nên bẻ lái thì tay theo), hai chân tới sàn để chân. Sai số bàn tay – tay nắm ≤ 2 cm, bàn chân – sàn ≤ 3 cm (test).
- Phản ứng (mẫu `pilot/react.ts`): thân trên nghiêng theo xe nhưng đầu giữ thẳng hơn (≈ 60 % độ nghiêng), ngả sau khi tăng tốc, chúi trước khi phanh, nhún theo giảm xóc; biên độ nhỏ, có lò xo.
- Mũ bảo hiểm nửa đầu dựng bằng code, gắn xương đầu (luật Việt Nam; cũng che tóc xuyên camera). **(Claude)**
- Góc nhìn thứ nhất: ẩn đầu + mũ của chính mình (thu xương đầu về scale ≈ 0), giữ thân, tay.
- Ban đêm người lái không được đen kịt (hạn chế đã biết của người treo dù): kiểm bằng ảnh.

## 7. Camera (`src/explore/bike/camera.ts`)
- **Thứ nhất (mặc định) (ND)**: điểm mắt là một điểm cố định trong hệ thân xe (trên yên ≈ 0,75 m, lùi sau cổ lái), không lấy từ xương đầu (tránh rung theo hoạt ảnh). Cao mắt so với mặt đường ≈ 1,45 m. `fov` ≈ 75° (ước lượng), mặt cắt gần hạ đủ để không cắt ghi đông (≈ 0,1 m; `stop()` trả lại giá trị cũ cùng `fov`).
  - Cuộn theo ≈ 60 % độ nghiêng xe (đầu người giữ thăng bằng), có lò xo; chúi / ngửa theo giảm xóc với hệ số < 1; rung mặt đường biên độ ≤ 1 cm và chỉ tăng nhẹ theo tốc độ; lùi nhẹ khi tăng tốc, dồn trước khi phanh (≤ 4 cm).
  - Kéo chuột / vuốt: nhìn quanh ±120° ngang, −40°..+30° dọc, thôi kéo thì tự về như `drCamDrag`.
  - Một hệ số `CONFIG.bike.cam.motion` (0..1) nhân mọi chuyển động phụ; `prefers-reduced-motion` ⇒ 0,3.
- **Thứ ba**: `drCamPlace` với bộ số của xe máy (gần và thấp hơn ô tô), nhận bộ số qua tham số thay vì đọc cứng `CONFIG.drive.cam`; giữ cắt theo vật cản và kẹp trần hầm. Cuộn theo ≈ 20 % độ nghiêng.
- Đổi góc nhìn: phím V / nút HUD; trộn vị trí + hướng trong ≈ 0,4 s, không dừng xe. Chế độ xem người khác luôn là thứ ba.
- Trong hầm và dưới gầm cầu, góc thứ nhất không cần cắt vật cản (camera nằm trong thân va chạm).

## 8. Âm thanh (`src/explore/bike/sound.ts`, dùng `audio.sfxPort()` / `extPort()` và nút 🔊 như ô tô)
- **Máy** **(ND)**: 3 đoạn thu CC0 (cầm chừng, tua thấp có tải, tua cao có tải) giải mã thành `AudioBuffer`, phát lặp có điểm lặp, trộn chéo theo `rpm` + `throttle`, `playbackRate` theo `rpm` trong ±20 % quanh tua gốc của mỗi đoạn. Tiếng đề máy khi vào, tắt máy khi thoát. Nguồn (ví dụ Freesound lọc CC0) do người làm tìm; **người dùng nghe duyệt** trước khi commit. Trần: tổng ≤ 400 kB, đặt ở `public/bike/snd/` kèm `LICENSE-Sounds.txt`. Tải lười khi vào chế độ; chưa về / lỗi ⇒ máy tổng hợp (răng cưa + nhiễu qua lọc) để không bao giờ câm.
- **Tổng hợp**: lốp (nhiễu lọc theo |v|), gió (nhiễu dải thông theo v², to hơn ở góc thứ nhất), phanh (rít nhẹ khi phanh mạnh ở tốc độ cao), giảm xóc (tiếng "cụp" nhỏ khi hành trình vượt ngưỡng), xi nhan (tích tắc), còi (hai nốt, cao hơn còi ô tô), mưa trên mũ khi trời mưa.
- **Theo vị trí**: tối đa 3 giọng cho xe tự động gần nhất từ `trNearby` (âm lượng theo khoảng cách, `StereoPannerNode` theo hướng tương đối, cao độ theo tốc độ tương đối); nền thành phố và nền sông trộn theo khoảng cách tới mép kè |x| = 262; trên cầu tăng gió. Trong ô `tunnel`: bật nhánh vọng (trễ có hồi tiếp qua lọc), chuyển mượt ≈ 0,5 s.
- Mọi tham số ghi tối đa mỗi `sound.updateMs`; `stop()` dừng và ngắt mọi nút, thả cổng riêng; vào lại không nhân đôi (test đếm nút sống).
- Không trần âm lượng nào vượt mức mô tơ ô tô hiện tại quá 6 dB; có nén (`DynamicsCompressorNode`) ở đầu ra riêng của chế độ để không vọt tiếng.

- **Mặt đồng hồ**: texture canvas (kim tốc độ theo `v` thật, kim tua, đèn xi nhan), vẽ lại tối đa 10 lần/giây, tự sáng ban đêm.
- **Gương**: vật liệu kim loại nhẵn nhận màu trời hiện tại (ngày xanh, đêm tối + ánh đèn ấm), không vẽ lại cảnh.

Điều kiện: +0 lệnh vẽ, số program không tăng ở `test:perf -- --strict`, góc cũ ban ngày trời khô nhìn từ xa không đổi thấy được. **Đây là phần rủi ro nhất** (đụng vật liệu dùng chung): làm thành mốc riêng, có cờ `CONFIG.bike.road.detail` / `wet` tắt được, và bỏ được mà không ảnh hưởng phần còn lại.
- **Bụi nước bánh xe**: một lưới hạt (một lệnh vẽ, chỉ khi mưa và v > ngưỡng), số hạt theo tốc độ × cường độ mưa, ngẫu nhiên từ `rng(seed)` riêng.
- Hạt mưa, sấm, gió: của hệ thời tiết sẵn có, không đổi. Bão: vẫn lái được; xe tự động theo luật sẵn có.
- Cầu Rồng phun, cầu quay ban đêm: `exNightStep(dt, false)` như ô tô.

## 11. Nhiều người
- Dùng chung 5 chỗ kind `drive` với Ô tô **(ND)**. `join` thêm `veh` (0 ô tô — mặc định khi vắng, 1 xe máy) và `ch` (nhân vật, như kind `walk`); máy chủ giữ theo slot (cả qua hibernation, như `ch` của D-039) và phát trong `lobby.drivers`; `joined` vọng lại `veh`.
- `pos` người lái giữ nguyên dạng `[slot, x, y, z, yaw, v, st, ts]`; với xe máy `st` mang độ nghiêng (rad) thay cho góc lái. Người làm kiểm khoảng kẹp `st` ở Worker có chứa ±0,7 rad.
- Tương thích: máy chủ cũ (không vọng `veh` trong `joined`) ⇒ khách rời chỗ và lái một mình, như quy tắc "máy chủ cũ không gửi `drivers`". Khách cũ thấy người đi xe máy thành một chiếc ô tô cho tới khi tải lại trang (chấp nhận).
- Hiển thị: `remoteDrive.ts` chọn hình theo `veh`; xe máy người khác = glb + người lái có xương ở tư thế ngồi, nghiêng theo `st`, không IK chân / phản ứng (rẻ), điện thoại dùng hình tạm. Nhãn tên trên đầu người lái; chấm trên bản đồ nhỏ như ô tô. Không va chạm với nhau.
- Sảnh: thẻ Xe máy mở sảnh lái (đếm chung "n/5" với ô tô) kèm bộ chọn nam / nữ; hết chỗ ⇒ xem (camera thứ ba bám xe đang xem, ô tô hay xe máy). Rời máy, mất kết nối, lời mời: như ô tô.
- Thoát: `leave` + gỡ xe + người lái của mình; không để lại hình mồ côi (test hai trình duyệt).
- **Deploy Worker `danang-sky` phải hỏi người dùng riêng**; trước đó xe máy chạy một mình.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. ## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` by its absolute path, from the
  working tree you're executing in — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (under `<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If one exists,
  read [references/resuming.md](references/resuming.md) before anything
  else: it says whose ledger it is and where to resume.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, read [references/preflight.md](references/preflight.md)
and run the conflict scan it describes. Its table and rulings go in the
ledger.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Small same-shape work:** when the plan lists several small edits of the
same kind across files, read [references/batching.md](references/batching.md)
before dispatching them.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` by its absolute path, from the
  working tree you're executing in — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` by its absolute path, from the working tree you're executing in — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**Any other status** (DONE_WITH_CONCERNS, NEEDS_CONTEXT, BLOCKED): read
[references/handling-reports.md](references/handling-reports.md) and follow
it, every time you get one.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` by its absolute path, from
  the working tree you're executing in, and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
If the reviewer reports "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items, read
[references/cannot-verify.md](references/cannot-verify.md) before you mark
the task complete.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

When it triggers, read [references/fix-loop.md](references/fix-loop.md) and
follow it. Read it again before every round, even if you read it earlier in
this session: it holds the round cap, the breaker, and the ledger line each
round writes, and your memory of it does not survive compaction.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

When every task is complete, read
[references/final-review.md](references/final-review.md) and follow it. It
covers the whole-branch review, its single fix wave, and how you finish.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |
| "The implementer spawned its own reviewer — free extra assurance" | It's a duplicate seat reviewing the same diff; the task review is the gate. A worker-spawned reviewer is a defect to flag, not rigor. |
